result.summary: A multi-dimensional table cannot remove bits at R=20. The reason is exact and countable: the whole per-context computation (three lookups, collapse, C3) depends on the digest and the eight context words only through FIVE 32-bit constants sigma = (KC0, KC1, KC2, v, kappa3) — verified 200/200 against the published code at full width and exhaustively at w=6,8. The solving a0 is a non-degenerate function of all five, so a universal table must be indexed by >=4.58 full-width axes; a 3-axis table, even at full 32-bit resolution (2^96 entries), aggregates 2^64 signatures per cell of which 2^50.6 are solvable, so its answer is "yes" for every cell: exactly 0 bits. Coarse grids are strictly worse, and any per-instance grid must be built by the 2^32 sweep it was meant to replace. C3 is not an inversion problem at all (W3 = kappa3 - sigma0(W4) is closed form) but a membership problem in an instance-specific set of 2^18.6 reachable (W3,W4) pairs — tables invert, they do not test membership in a set indexed by 128 context bits. The one genuine 2D table in the family, index (target, root number) of sigma0(u)-u, is already 93% exploited: root multiplicity is Poisson(1), so a complete multi-root table is worth 0.099 bits. MITM: no split exists on the unknown side (c3's mixed second difference is nonzero in 65536/65536 trials at every 2-way split of a0..a3, 16/32 bits moved, not even bit 0 separable). The only real split is context-vs-list, and it is the amortisation the project already knows: it would be worth 31 bits at R=20 and 31.6 at R=21, but a fibre member costs 2^47.5 at best against a break-even of exactly 2^32. k-list: the fourth constraint is a 2SUM with a single index; matching is already free and generation is the bottleneck, so no k>1 exists, and the generic MITM/Wagner bounds (2^64 at R=20, 2^96 at R=21) are worse than the published attack.
result.mechanism:
EXACT ALGEBRA. After the per-context constants are folded, attack_context uses only KC0 (target offset of the C0 lookup), KC1, KC2, v = a4 (the collapse parameter), and kappa3 = W19 - sigma1(W17) - W12, plus the IV. Stage 1 target = KC0 - W0(a0) - G(a0); stage 2 = KC1 - W1 - F12(a0,a1); stage 3 = KC2 - W2 - F23(a0,a1,a2); collapse = Maj(v,a3,a2)==a3; c3 = sigma0(W4)+W3-kappa3. So the attack is a map (a0, sigma) -> {0,1} with sigma a 5-word signature, and the 160 bits of context freedom (v,a6,a7,a10,a11 at R=20; +a12 at R=21) map onto those 160 bits with full avalanche (11-16 of 32 bits changed per flipped input bit; no neutral word, no triangularity).

(a) TABLE DIMENSION. A table removes work only when its index determines the answer. Fraction of signatures admitting a solution = c^3 (3/4)^32 = 2^-13.38. A table with k full-width axes has cells aggregating 2^(160-32k) signatures; the cell can say "no solution" only if 2^(160-32k) <= 2^13.38, i.e. k >= 4.58 -> k = 5 axes = 2^160 entries. k=3 (2^96 entries) leaves 2^50.6 solvable signatures per cell: zero information, at any resolution b <= 32 per axis. Quantisation is not the issue; dimension is. Separately, a per-context 3D grid over (W3,W4) or (a0,W3,W4) is buildable only by the sweep itself, so it reorganises but never reduces it. And C3 needs no inversion — the useful contrast is that C0/C1/C2 each reduce to the parameter-free universal relation sigma0(u)-u = t (one coordinate, 2^32 entries, a perfect TMTO point), whereas the C3 residual after the third lookup is a one-variable equation whose parameters are (a0,a1,a2,v) = 128 bits, so the analogous table is 2^128.

(b) MITM. Unknown side: c0 involves (a0,a1), c1 (a0,a1,a2), c2 and c3 all four; a0 feeds both W3 and W4 as suspected, and c3's mixed second difference over {a0}, {a1}, {a2}, {a3}, {a0,a1}, {a0,a2}, {a0,a3} versus the rest is nonzero in 65536/65536 trials at w=32 (mean 16/32 bits moved), with 0 separable low bits — Maj/Ch mix the unknowns bitwise before any carry, so even the carry-free LSB does not split. No split exists.
Context side: contexts sharing (KC0,KC1,KC2,v) share the entire candidate list, so one sweep answers all of them; each fibre member then costs O(1) instead of 2^32. Cost/preimage = P^-1 (2^32/m + X), P = 2^-13.38 (R=20) or 2^-45.38 (R=21), X = cost of one fibre member. With X = 1 and the full fibre (2^32 at R=20, 2^64 at R=21) this gives 2^14.4 (31.0 bits) and 2^45.4 (32.0 bits) — the R=21 figure is exactly the ~30-bit target. Break-even is X = 2^32 at both rounds. Fibre sampling is forward-only: the map (a6,a7,a10,a11) -> (KC0,KC1,KC2) has full avalanche, no additive or XOR separability at any 2-way split (65536/65536 nonzero second differences at w=32), Poisson fibre sizes (chi^2 = 52.7 on 57 df, exhaustive over all 2^24 contexts at w=6), no signature-preserving shift (the top recurring within-fibre shifts retest at 0.89-1.38x chance over all 2^24 contexts), no affine fibre (0/50), and a perfectly flat partial-match landscape (matches on k bits track 2^(4w-k) at every k, w=8). Hence X = 2^96 generically; the cheapest achievable is the m=2 birthday, X = 2^47.5, which is 15.5 bits above break-even and gives 2^60.9 at R=20 — reproducing the elimination search's independently derived 2^60.4 — and 2^92.9 at R=21. Even a hypothetical perfectly separable map (2-list MITM, X = 2^48) or a fully triangular one (three exhaustive 32-bit solves, X = 2^32) only ties. Conservation law over the frame family: absorbing j constraints by lookup makes the sweep 2^(32(4-j)) and the signature 32j bits, so the reuse birthday cost is 2^(16j) and reuse pays only for j <= 2 — but j=2 costs 2^78.6 baseline and 2^49.4 storage. j=3 is optimal and unreusable.

(c) k-LIST. c3 = sigma0(W4) + W3 - kappa3 is formally a 2SUM over Z/2^32, but (W3,W4) is a function of the single index a0, so there is exactly one list. k-list algorithms accelerate matching in a large candidate space; here matching is already O(1) per candidate and the bottleneck is generation — 2^32 swept a0 produce only 2^18.6 candidates against a 2^32 condition. Un-triangularising to four free unknowns and four 32-bit constraints (128 bits): 2-list MITM = 2^64 (18.6 bits worse than 2^45.4), Wagner k=4 needs lists of 2^42.7 while each unknown supplies only 2^32, and k=8 needs eight independent lists where only four unknowns exist. At R=21 (160 bits): MITM 2^96, Wagner k=4 needs 2^53.3. All of it presupposes additive separability, which is measurably absent. The published attack already beats every generic k-list bound because triangularity plus a universal inversion is strictly stronger than a birthday match.

result.summary:
The 3D-state / symmetry reading is closed, gain 0 bits, and it is closed twice over: once a priori by a ceiling argument, once empirically by measurement.

CEILING (the decisive point, and it is unconditional). A symmetry sigma maps preimages of H to preimages of sigma(H). For a FIXED target it removes bits only if sigma(H) = H, and then it removes at most log2|Stab(H)| bits by quotienting the search to a fundamental domain. The candidate groups are tiny: bit rotations |G| <= 32 (5 bits), complementation |G| = 2 (1 bit), round-axis translation |G| <= 20 (4.32 bits). Even if every one of them were free, exact, and target-stabilising simultaneously, the total is log2(32*2*20) = 10.3 bits against the ~30 bits R=21 needs. The entire reading is capped at a third of the requirement before a single line of code runs. This is worth recording in the barrier paper: it retires the whole symmetry direction, not just the instances tested.

Every instance then dies anyway, each at a named component:

(a) COMMUTATION WITH A BIT-AXIS ROTATION. Exact: Sigma0, Sigma1 (XOR of three rotations), Ch, Maj, XOR all commute (P = 1 on 2^22 samples). Broken: sigma0, sigma1, by their SHR terms only. The defect obeys an exact law I verified exhaustively over all (w,s,g) at w = 6,8,12,16,32,64 (5350 cases, 0 mismatches): the defect of (x>>s)<<<g vs (x<<<g)>>s occupies exactly 2*min(g, s, w-g, w-s) bit positions, so P[commute] = 2^-2*min(...). At w=32, g=1 that is 2^-2 for both sigma0 and sigma1. Modular addition follows Daum's law P = (1/4)(1 + 2^(g-32) + 2^-g + 2^-32), max 0.375 = 2^-1.415 at g = 1 or 31, confirmed to every digit exhaustively at w = 8 and w = 12.

Strongest single structural statement: the bit-axis symmetry group of SHA-256's GF(2)-linear layer is TRIVIAL. Over the full dihedral group of the bit axis (32 rotations x bit-reversal), exactly one element — the identity — commutes with all of Sigma0, Sigma1, sigma0, sigma1 simultaneously. All 32 rotations commute with Sigma0 and Sigma1; none commutes with sigma0 or sigma1. The killing component is the SHR term in the message expansion, before any constant or carry enters.

MESSAGE SCHEDULE ALONE, CONSTANTS REMOVED (the measurement asked for). P[W16 stays a rotational pair] = 0.039095 = 2^-4.677 at g = 1 (2^24 pairs). Through W16..W19, the four words R = 20 needs: 1.97e-6 = 2^-18.95. For g = 2, 3, 8, 16, 30 it is 0 in 2^24 samples by W18 at the latest (g=2 already 2^-8.9 at W16 alone). Only g = 1 and 31 survive at all. Validated on a reduced-width analogue: exhaustively over all 2^24 inputs of a w = 6 schedule step, P = 0.0390625 = 2^-4.678, the same value as the 32-bit sampled one, so the mechanism is width-independent. Note the naive factorisation P[sigma0]*P[sigma1]*P[4-term add] = 0.0095 underestimates by ~4x: the shift defects and the carry conditions are dependent, both living at the word ends.

(b) SYMMETRIES MAPPING PREIMAGES TO PREIMAGES. All four tested, all dead.

Rotation. Two independent kills. First the target: the feed-forward h_i = IV_i + s_i means a state rotation acts on the digest as h_i -> rot_g(h_i - IV_i) + IV_i, so a target is stabilised only if every s_i = h_i - IV_i is rotation-invariant. Both published 20-round targets have stabiliser exactly 1. This includes the all-ones digest, which is the case where the orbit argument would have bitten — ff..ff is rotation-invariant as a bit string, and Zaikin chose it for its symmetry — but the required final state is s_i = ~IV_i, and none of the eight words ~IV_i has any nontrivial rotational period. The IV feed-forward is the killing component there. Globally only a 2^-128 fraction of digests (at g = 16; 2^-248 at g = 1) has any nontrivial stabiliser. Second the trail: with all constants removed and the chaining value rotated, the per-round survival is 2^-5.49 (2^24 samples, g = 1 and 31; 2^-13.7 at g = 2, 2^-22 at g = 16), i.e. ~2^-110 over 20 rounds, times 2^-19 for the schedule. With the real IV and K it is not small but exactly zero: exhaustively over all 2^32 values of W0, for every g in {1,2,3,8,16,24,31}, ZERO choices make round 0 rotational. Concretely, rotating either published preimage's message matches 0 of 4 expanded words and 0 of 40 state words.

Complementation. Killed by Ch, and by nothing else. Sigma0, Sigma1, Maj are self-dual (P = 1); sigma0 and sigma1 have a CONSTANT defect (0xe0000000, 0xffc00000) so they are harmless; modular addition is exactly affine under complementation (~x + ~y = ~(x+y) - 1, P = 1 always). But Ch(~e,~f,~g) = ~Ch(e,f,g) on exactly 4 of the 8 bit patterns, so 2^-32 per word, measured 0 of 2^22. Ch is the unique non-self-dual component of SHA-256.

Symmetric states (words of bit period d | 32, the Keccak CP-kernel analogue). Sigma0/Sigma1/Ch/Maj preserve the period-d subspace exactly; addition leaves it with P ~ 0.5-0.75; sigma0 leaves it with P = 0.125 at every d, sigma1 with P = 0.0010 at d = 16. And no K_r has any bit period d | 32, no K_r and no IV word has any nontrivial rotational symmetry, and no K_r is self-complementary (0 of 64, 0 of 8, 0 of 64). Separately, restricting the sweep to a period-d subset is an instance of the density-2^-k table policy already proved zero-sum in elimination_search/FINDINGS.md: it buys k bits of structure in W3 and loses exactly 2^-k in lookup hit rate.

THE ATTACK-SPECIFIC RESULT, which is the interesting one. The submask family is by far the most symmetry-friendly object in this project, and it still fails. a4 = a5 is covariant under any word map; e8 = e9 = 0xFFFFFFFF is literally a symmetric state (all-ones is rotation-invariant); and the collapsed condition Maj(v,a3,a2) = a3 is purely bitwise, hence invariant under EVERY bit permutation (measured exactly 1.000000). Three of the four family conditions are free. It dies on the fourth: rotating a family context leaves e8 = e9 = -1 with probability only 2.1e-2 at g = 1 and 1.5e-3 at g = 16, because the construction a8 = -1 - a4 + Sigma0(a7) + Maj(a7,a6,a5) is a modular sum; and c3 = sigma0(W4) + W3 - kappa3 is covariant with probability 0.1875 = 2^-2.4 at g = 1, plus a deterministic mismatch rot(kappa3) != kappa3. So the symmetry dies at exactly the same wall as everything else in this project: sigma0/Sigma0 of an unknown plus a sum mod 2^32. It is the offset law again, wearing different clothes.

Also measured, since the 3D view suggests it: the 16 GB table map u -> sigma0(u) - u is rotation-covariant with probability 2^-2 at g = 1 (the subtraction contributes nothing beyond sigma0's own defect), so no 32x table compression exists; and even a FREE 32x compression is worth at most log2(1/0.9337) = 0.099 bits, since it could only raise three-root coverage from 0.9337 to 1.

(c) SLIDE / TRANSLATION ALONG THE ROUND AXIS. Half of it is free and that is worth knowing: the message expansion is a constant-coefficient recurrence, hence EXACTLY translation-covariant — W'_i = W_(i+d) is again a valid schedule, at probability 1. The obstructions are precisely two, and both are hard. K_r = K_(r+d) holds for 0 of 63 pairs at every d = 1..20, and all 20 constants used at R = 20 are distinct. And the IV: a d = 1 slide needs the state after round 1 to equal the IV, which forces six word equalities among the IV (IV0=IV1, IV1=IV2, IV2=IV3, IV4=IV5, IV5=IV6, IV6=IV7); 0 of 6 hold, so a d = 1 slide is IMPOSSIBLE, not rare — probability 0, not 2^-k. For d >= 4 all eight state words are message-dependent, so a slid pair is 8 x 32 = 256 bit conditions, harder than the preimage itself, and even then it relates preimages of two DIFFERENT digests, which re-enters the stabiliser requirement of the ceiling. This is the classical defence working exactly as designed: SHA-1 reuses one constant for 20 consecutive rounds; SHA-256 uses 64 distinct ones.

(d) THE MODERN REFINEMENT, WHICH IS WHAT WOULD RESCUE THIS IF ANYTHING COULD. "Constants break rotational symmetry" is a 2010 statement; rotational-XOR (RX) cryptanalysis was invented precisely to absorb constants into a fixed XOR difference, so I tested it rather than asserting the old story. Two measurements close it. First, exhaustively over ALL RX-difference triples at w = 6, 7, 8 and gamma = 1, 2, the ZERO RX-difference is optimal for modular addition — best p is attained at (d1,d2,d3) = (0,0,0) and equals the plain Daum value. RX therefore can never beat the constant-free rotational trail per addition; it can only try to restore what the constants destroy. Second, it cannot even do that here: the best RX probability for x -> x + K_r at gamma = 1, optimising the output difference, is between 2^-9.15 and 2^-13.69 across the twenty real constants, and their product is 2^-207 for R = 20 — from the constants alone, before the other 120 additions and the schedule. The mechanism is density: SHA-256's K_r have mean Hamming weight exactly 16.0 of 32 (they are fractional parts of cube roots of primes), so the carry defect under +K_r is data-dependent with 10^5 to 10^6 distinct values per constant, and no fixed delta absorbs it. The contrast with Keccak is quantitative, not rhetorical: iota touches 1 lane of 25 and its constants have mean Hamming weight 3.3 of 64, which is why rotational cryptanalysis reached a 5-round distinguisher and a 4-round preimage there and reaches zero rounds here.

Caveat stated honestly: the RX constant measurement fixed the incoming difference to zero and optimised only the outgoing one; a full two-sided RX-trail search was not run. The blocking mechanism — a data-dependent carry defect with ~10^5 distinct values — is not something the incoming delta changes in character, and the exhaustive reduced-width result says zero is optimal for the addition itself, so I do not expect it to matter. But it is not proved.

Bottom line: 0 bits, and the reading should be recorded as closed by the ceiling rather than by the measurements, because the ceiling is the part that generalises.
result.mechanism:
Two independent mechanisms, one a priori and one measured.

A PRIORI (the ceiling). For a fixed-target preimage attack, a symmetry group G removes bits only through orbit-quotienting, which requires the target to be stabilised and yields at most log2|Stab(H)| bits. The available groups are of order 32 (bit rotation), 2 (complementation) and <= 20 (round-axis translation), so the direction is capped at 10.3 bits against a 30-bit requirement, regardless of how well any symmetry propagates. No amount of trail engineering can exceed a group-order bound.

MEASURED (why each symmetry is not even free). Three named killers, in order of how early they fire:

1. The SHR terms of sigma0 and sigma1. These are the reason the bit-axis symmetry group of SHA-256's linear layer is trivial: all 32 rotations commute with Sigma0 and Sigma1, none commutes with sigma0 or sigma1. This fires before any constant or carry, and it is what costs 2^-4.68 per expanded word (2^-19 through W16..W19). Exact law, exhaustively verified at six widths: the defect spans 2*min(g,s,w-g,w-s) bit positions.

2. The carries of addition mod 2^32. Daum's law caps a single addition at 2^-1.415 (g = 1), and the exhaustive reduced-width RX search shows no XOR difference beats it, so this cost is irreducible even in the RX framework. SHA-256 has 7 additions per round; measured per-round survival is 2^-5.49.

3. The constants, in two roles. The round constants K_r are dense (mean Hamming weight 16.0/32) so their RX cost is 2^-207 over R = 20; and the IV feed-forward h_i = IV_i + s_i is what destroys the target's stabiliser, including for the all-ones digest, whose required state ~IV has no rotational symmetry in any of its eight words.

For complementation the killer is different and specific: Ch is the unique non-self-dual component (Sigma0, Sigma1, Maj are self-dual, sigma0/sigma1 have constant defects, and addition is exactly affine under x -> ~x). For the slide the killers are the 20 distinct K_r and six false word equalities in the IV.

Within the attack itself the failure localises to the same place as the offset law: the submask family's a4 = a5, e8 = e9 = -1 and the bitwise collapse Maj(v,a3,a2) = a3 are all symmetry-covariant for free, and the construction breaks only where a context word passes through Sigma0 into a modular sum (a8 = -1 - a4 + Sigma0(a7) + Maj(...)) and where c3 = sigma0(W4) + W3 - kappa3 mixes a shift with a sum mod 2^32. One-input rotate-XOR-shift functions composed with carries: the same wall, reached from a new direction.

result.mechanism:
Four measured layers.

(1) ENCODING IS FREE, GEOMETRY IS NOT. Bit-blasting is exact and cheap: a+b+c = x + 2m with x,m in {0,1} simultaneously defines XOR and Maj; AND is Maj with c=0; Ch = g^(e&(f^g)) is three such gadgets; addition mod 2^w is a carry chain. Every gadget was validated against a planted solution. But each gadget contributes 2w new 0/1 variables against only w new equations. Hence N ~ 2M always, dim(L0) = N+1-rank ~ N/2, and det(L0)^(1/dim) converges to a constant ~2.5. So the Gaussian heuristic of the solution lattice is Theta(1) while the centred target vector (all coordinates +-1) has norm sqrt(N+1) = Theta(sqrt N). The ratio ||target||/gh therefore tends to sqrt(2*2*pi*e)/2.5 = 2.3 at EVERY width and for EVERY subsystem, and the number of lattice points at least as short as the solution is 2^(1.2*dim).

(2) WHAT THE SHORT VECTORS ARE. Inspected directly at w=8: the shortest vector of the solution lattice has squared norm 6 (against the solution's 33) and is a carry re-encoding -- y_7 -= 2, t_7 += 1, b_8 += 1. It satisfies every equation exactly and leaves {0,1} only in the range, which the Euclidean norm cannot see. The lattice keeps the linear algebra and throws away exactly the constraint that carries all the nonlinearity.

(3) NO WORD-LEVEL LATTICE. A word-level (Coppersmith/BDD/truncated-LCG) formulation needs sigma0(x) = alpha*x + beta + e(x) with e confined to a short arc. Exhaustively over ALL alpha in Z/2^w the shortest arc containing e(x) is 238/256 (w=8, 7.89 bits), 4039/4096 (w=12, 11.98 bits), 65494/65536 (w=16, 16.00 bits), and 4,293,693,282/2^32 (w=32, sampled alphas, 32.00 bits). The error fills the modulus; there is no small root. The one set on which sigma0 is exactly Z-linear (the carry-free set, where the three rotated copies are pairwise disjoint) contains exactly 62,129 of 2^32 words = 15.92 bits, so restricting a0..a3 to it leaves 64 bits of entropy against 128 bits of constraint: overdetermined, no solution survives.

(4) THE INFORMATION-THEORETIC ROOT CAUSE -- NO FREE REDUNDANCY. Calibrated by positive controls run through the identical code path, LLL succeeds iff ratio < 1: low-density subset sum n=40 gives 15/20 at ratio 0.40 and 0/20 from ratio 1.01 upward; truncated LCG (q=2^32, 8 outputs) gives 18/20 at k=4 unknown bits, 8/20 at k=8, 2/20 at k=12, 0/20 from k=16. At R=20 with the context fixed the attack has 128 unknown bits (a0..a3) against 128 constraint bits (C0..C3): density exactly 1. To reach the density ~0.4 where LLL works one must leave about 51 unknown bits, at which point the expected number of solutions is 2^(51-128) = 2^-77, i.e. 2^77 contexts must be tried to manufacture one solvable instance. The 2^32 you want to remove reappears as the price of the redundancy. Lattices break truncated LCGs (more outputs are free), low-density knapsacks (modulus chosen much larger than the item count) and Coppersmith instances (|root| < q^(1/d)) because in all three the unknown is small relative to the modulus AND the redundancy is given away. In a SHA-256 preimage the equations ARE the goal, not free side information, and each extra round contributes one extra constraint together with one extra free word. This is the same wall the offset law describes, seen from the information side.

The closest relative is coding-theoretic rather than lattice-based: Pramstaller, Rechberger and Rijmen, "Exploiting Coding Theory for Collision Attacks on SHA-1" (2005), and Rechberger's "Preliminary Analysis of the SHA-256 Message Expansion" (NIST 2005) / Mendel-Pramstaller-Rechberger-Rijmen on step-reduced SHA-256, which search for low-weight codewords of the XOR-LINEARISED message expansion using probabilistic coding algorithms, not LLL; their stated limit -- "due to the nonlinear behaviour of the modular addition, no linear code can describe the SHA-256 message expansion" -- is the same obstruction measured here. The methods that do attack this exact 0/1 linear system are SAT/SMT (Zaikin's Transalg CNF for preimages; Nejati-Ganesh programmatic SAT for SHA-256 collisions) and MILP (Liu et al.'s MILP method for SHA-2 characteristics; MILP-based MITM preimage search on AES-like hashing, eprint 2024/300 and 2024/349). Both retain the {0,1} constraints as clauses or inequalities. The lattice relaxation is precisely the step that discards them, which is why it is strictly weaker here. Sources: https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/032.pdf , https://csrc.nist.rip/groups/ST/hash/documents/Rechberger_PreliminaryAnalysisOfSHA256.pdf , https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220963039_Exploiting_Coding_Theory_for_Collision_Attacks_on_SHA-1 , https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.20072 , https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/300.pdf , https://thomas-plantard.github.io/pdf/PlaSusZha12.pdf , https://simons.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/docs/14975/cryptanalysis.pdf

No further lattice work is warranted; this line is closed and I would not spend another CPU-hour on it. What is worth keeping is the SCREENING TEST, because it makes any future lattice proposal falsifiable in minutes rather than days. For any proposed embedding of any SHA-256 subproblem, build the 0/1 system, compute dim L0 = N+1-rank(A), det(L0) = sqrt(det(Abar Abar^T)) (validated exactly against LLL at w=8,12,16), gh = sqrt(dim/2 pi e) det^(1/dim), and ratio = sqrt(N+1)/gh. The controls fix the decision boundary at ratio = 1: subset sum succeeds at 0.40 and fails at 1.01. Every SHA-256 formulation I built lands at 2.25-2.38. A proposal that does not get below 1 does not need to be run, and one that does get below 1 must be reported together with the expected solution count, because the two move against each other -- that is the actual barrier. Scripts e4_geom.py and blast.py already accept a new system in the (A, b) form.

If the author nevertheless wants one more falsification attempt on my own conclusion, the honest one is not a lattice but the natural control the SAT study left open: blast.py emits the full R=20 problem as a 3,936-variable / 1,536-constraint 0/1 integer program with all coefficients in {-2,-1,1,2}, which is exactly the shape MILP and pseudo-Boolean solvers are built for and which retains the {0,1} ranges as inequalities. Running that through a MILP or PB solver for a day, against the 12 ms the table attack takes on the same instance, would close the "different mathematical technique" question from the optimisation side as the sat_hybrid study closed it from the CDCL side. My prediction, from the fact that the CDCL encoding of the identical instance does not finish in 1800 s, is that it gains nothing.

One measurement I could not complete and would flag as genuinely untested rather than excluded: the maximum modular-additive correlation of sigma0 at the true width. It is 0.32-0.37 at w=8,12,16 by exhaustive FFT, well above the 2^-w/2 noise floor, and I could not compute it at w=32 (a 2^32-point complex FFT does not fit here). It does not bound the error range, so it cannot revive a lattice, and it is worth only about 0.15 bits as a bias; but if anyone wants a loose end, that is the one, and it costs a machine with ~128 GB rather than a new idea.

result.verdict:
**gain_bits = 0.** The "3D lattice" intuition is closed, and closed harder than the previous dead ends — but it failed for a reason nobody predicted, and that reason is worth more than the negative result.

Four readings of your question were run (lattice reduction proper; multi-dimensional tables; geometric/symmetry structure; the integer-programming/Gröbner/linearisation wildcard). All four returned 0 bits at R=20 and at R=21, and all four terminate at the same place the previous six searches did: a one-input rotate-XOR function of an unknown (Sigma0/sigma0) composed with addition mod 2^32. That is the offset law, and it is now reached from four new directions rather than one.

I re-derived or independently recomputed four of the load-bearing numbers rather than take them on trust:
- carry-free set of sigma0 at w=32: my own exhaustive 2^32 scan gives **exactly 62,129** (2^15.92) — the lattice study's figure, to the unit;
- the "structural constant" ratio 2.30–2.38: analytically sqrt(4·pi·e)/2.5 = **2.3378**, which explains why the same number appears in all twelve measured cells and confirms it is a property of the 0/1-with-carry-gadget encoding, not of a width or a subsystem;
- word-level linearity: my exhaustive min-arc over all alpha gives 239/256 (7.90 bits) and 4040/4096 (11.98 bits), against their 238/4039 — an off-by-one arc convention, identical conclusion (**no small root exists, so no Coppersmith/BDD shape exists**);
- constants audit: 0 of 64 K_r rotation-invariant, 0 of 8 IV words, 0 of 8 complemented IV words, 0 adjacent-equal K_r, 20 distinct K_r at R=20, ceiling log2(32·2·20) = 10.32 — all confirmed.

Two corrections you should make before any of this is quoted, neither fatal:
1. **The symmetry study's "K_r have mean Hamming weight exactly 16.0 of 32" is true only of the 20 constants used at R=20.** Over all 64 the mean is 15.52. The Keccak contrast (3.33 of 64, on 1 lane of 25) survives untouched, but the sentence as written is refutable by a referee with a calculator.
2. **The multidim-table study's headline R=20 amortisation figure, 2^14.4, is the cost per preimage only if you harvest all ~2^18.6 preimages of one digest from a single fibre.** For one preimage of one prescribed digest the mandatory sweep is a hard floor: cost = 2^32 + 2^13.38·X, so the R=20 payoff under perfect fibre reuse is **13.4 bits, not 31**. Their R=21 figure (2^45.4 at X=1) is correct, because there the 2^45.38·X term dominates the 2^32 floor. This matters: it halves the advertised prize at R=20 and leaves R=21 as the only place the idea is worth anything.

Cross-corroboration worth recording: two studies that did not share code derived the m=2 fibre-amortisation cost independently and agree (elimination_search 2^60.4, multidim-tables 2^60.88), and three independent measurements of context-word avalanche agree (10.6–16.1, 10.9–16.1, 11.28–16.01 bits per flipped bit). That is the kind of agreement that makes a negative trustworthy.
result.per_reading:
**1. Lattice reduction — 0 bits. Obstruction: the relaxation discards the {0,1} ranges, and the system's density is exactly 1.**
The expected diagnosis was "SHA-256 cannot be encoded in a lattice". That is **wrong**, and finding it wrong is the most interesting thing in the study. Encoding is exact and cheap: a+b+c = x+2m with x,m in {0,1} simultaneously defines XOR and Maj, so every SHA-256 primitive (Sigma/sigma, Maj, AND, Ch, addition mod 2^32) is exactly Z-linear in 0/1 variables. The failure is geometric. Each carry gadget adds 2w variables against w equations, so N ≈ 2M always, dim ≈ N/2, det^(1/dim) → 2.5, and hence ||target||/gh → sqrt(4·pi·e)/2.5 = 2.34 at **every** width and for **every** subsystem — I verified that identity analytically, which is why it is a constant and not an artefact. Since LLL succeeds iff that ratio is below 1 (calibrated against subset-sum at 0.40 succeeding and 1.01 failing, and truncated LCG at k=4 succeeding and k=16 failing, through the same code path), the failure is not reduction quality: a **perfect SVP oracle** fails, because ~2^76 lattice points are at least as short as the solution for the single sigma0 inversion and ~2^2891 for the full C0..C3 system. The shortest vector was inspected at w=8: squared norm 6, support {y_7 -= 2, t_7 += 1, b_8 += 1} — a carry re-encoding that satisfies every equation and violates only the range. Measured 0/50 LLL, 0/15 BKZ-20, 0/20 at w=32, two embeddings, and 0/10 even when handed 30 of 32 unknown bits. No word-level escape either (min-arc = the whole modulus, my check above). Information-theoretic root cause: lattices break truncated LCGs, low-density knapsacks and Coppersmith instances because redundancy is *given away free*; in a preimage the equations **are** the goal, 128 unknown bits against 128 constraint bits, density exactly 1, and buying the density-0.4 a lattice needs costs 2^77 contexts to manufacture one solvable instance. The 2^32 you wanted to delete reappears as the price of the redundancy. This is the offset law seen from the information side.

**2. Multi-dimensional tables — 0 bits. Obstruction: a counting bound on table dimension, and C3 is a membership question, not an inversion.**
The whole per-context computation depends on the digest and all eight context words through only **five** 32-bit constants (KC0, KC1, KC2, v, kappa3) — verified 200/200 against the production code at full width and exhaustively at w=6,8. Since the solvable fraction of signatures is 2^-13.38, a table with k full-width axes has cells aggregating 2^(160-32k) signatures and can only answer "no" if k >= 4.58; a 3-axis table at full 32-bit resolution (2^96 entries) still says "yes" in every cell. Dimension, not resolution, is the barrier, so coarse grids are strictly worse and per-instance grids must be built by the sweep they were meant to replace. C3 is not invertible-by-table at all: W3 = kappa3 - sigma0(W4) is closed form; the question is *membership* in an instance-specific set of 2^18.6 reachable (W3,W4) pairs indexed by 128 context bits. The one real 2D table (target, root number) is already 93% exploited — root multiplicity is Poisson(1), ceiling 0.099 bits. MITM on the unknown side does not exist: the mixed second difference of c3 is nonzero in 65536/65536 trials at every 2-way split of a0..a3, with not even bit 0 separable, because Maj/Ch mix the unknowns bitwise *before* any carry. The one real split is context-vs-list, which is the amortisation lead below.

**3. Geometry / symmetry — 0 bits, and closed twice.**
The decisive part is a priori and unconditional: a symmetry helps a *fixed-target* preimage only by quotienting to a fundamental domain, which needs sigma(H) = H and yields at most log2|Stab(H)| bits. The available groups are order 32 (bit rotation), 2 (complementation), <= 20 (round translation): **10.32 bits total against the 30 that R=21 needs**, before any code runs. Every instance then dies anyway, each at a named component: the **SHR terms** of sigma0/sigma1 make the bit-axis symmetry group of SHA-256's linear layer exactly trivial (all 32 rotations commute with Sigma0 and Sigma1; none with sigma0 or sigma1), at 2^-4.68 per expanded word; the **carries** cap one addition at Daum's 2^-1.415; the **constants** in two roles — dense K_r give RX cost 2^-207 over 20 rounds, and the IV feed-forward destroys the target's stabiliser, *including for the all-ones digest*, whose required final state is ~IV and none of whose eight words has any rotational period. That last point is the one that would have bitten, and it is dead. Sharpest single measurement: over **all 2^32 values of W0**, real IV and K, there are **zero** rotational pairs even at round 0, for every rotation amount — impossible, not improbable. Complementation dies at Ch, the unique non-self-dual component. Slides die on 20 distinct K_r and six false IV word equalities (d=1 is impossible, probability 0). RX cryptanalysis, the modern refinement that exists precisely to absorb constants, was tested rather than dismissed: exhaustively at w=6,7,8 the zero RX-difference is optimal for modular addition, so RX can never beat the constant-free rotational trail. And the attack-specific result is the sharp one: three of the four family conditions are symmetry-free (a4=a5 covariant, e8=e9=-1 literally a symmetric state, the collapse invariant under every bit permutation at exactly 1.000000), and it still dies — on a8 = -1 - a4 + Sigma0(a7) + Maj(...) and on c3. **Sigma0 of an unknown into a sum mod 2^32, again.** One caution on the proposed Section 7 wording: the ceiling bounds *quotienting*, which is the right scope, so keep the sentence scoped that way; it does not by itself cover symmetry used to structure a search space, and it is the measurements that close that.

**4. Wildcard (integer programming / Gröbner / linearisation) — 0 bits. Obstruction: the offset law relocated inside C3 itself.**
This is the reading that names *why* the one collapse you already have cannot be repeated. A residual's zero set factors into independent per-bit conditions — the only known way to beat a 2^-32 filter, and exactly what bought you (3/4)^32 — only if it is built from **bitwise atoms**: eps = Maj(v,a3,a2) - a3 is identity and Maj, and borrow-free. The fourth residual, verified exactly at w=32, is c3 = kappa3 - sigma0(W4) - a3 + Sigma0(a2) + Maj(a2,a1,a0) + e_-1 + Sigma1(e2) + Ch(e2,e1,e0) + K3: **five rotate-XOR atoms whose arguments are functions of the unknowns alone**. Rotate-XOR mixes bit positions, so factorisation is destroyed; and being one-input, there is no second argument a context word could saturate. The scan that establishes this has a working positive control — it rediscovers the known collapse at exactly (3/2)^w at w=6,8,10 — and finds 0.996–1.048 times uniform in all 216 free-triple and 324 free-pair cells containing c3, flat in w. Beyond that: on the candidate manifold every Z-combination of C0..C3 reduces to lambda3·c3 (1683 real candidates from the production attack with the 16 GB table, 0 exceptions), so the family's constraint basis is unique up to sign among lookup-solvable combinations. CP-SAT on the exact instance the attack solves scales as 2^(1.86w) against the attack's 2^w, extrapolating to 2^63.5 branches / 2^50 seconds, with the LP relaxation worth at most 1.8x. The natural-variable ANF has density 0.4999 and near-maximal degree (~2^127 monomials per equation); the carry-augmented quadratic system is n=3331, m=4355 with d_reg = 257 and F4/F5 cost 2^2601 — even the unattainable idealisation of 128 quadratics in 128 unknowns gives 2^138, worse than brute force. The exact Walsh spectrum does find genuine linear structure in c3 (3–14x the random floor, far above a matched control) — but it totals **0.028 bits** and lives on a distribution the attack never samples.

**One cross-report resolution worth acting on:** the lattice study's proposed falsification (run the blasted 3,936-variable / 1,536-constraint 0/1 program through MILP or a pseudo-Boolean solver, since those retain the {0,1} ranges the lattice discards) has in effect **already been run** by the wildcard study — CP-SAT on the same instance, 2^(1.86w) scaling, 3 of 5 unsolved at w=8. Do not spend the day on it.
result.best_lead:
**One lead survives, and it is not a lattice.** It is the fibre-amortisation instance, proposed independently by the multi-dimensional-table study and priced independently by the elimination search. State it precisely, because the payoff is large at R=21 and the previously advertised R=20 payoff is half what was claimed.

**The instance.** Contexts sharing (KC0, KC1, KC2, v) share the *entire* candidate list — verified 18/18 byte-identical at w=8 and exhaustively over all 2^24 contexts at w=6, where one sweep per distinct signature found 248,957 preimages against 250,047 predicted, agreeing with individually swept contexts 40,000/40,000. kappa3 is *not* part of that signature, so each further context in the fibre gets a fresh, independent 2^-32 shot at C3 from the same list. Hash the ~2^18.6 candidate values of S = sigma0(W4) + W3 once; each new context's kappa3 is then a single probe, so the per-member *test* cost genuinely is O(1) and X is purely the cost of **producing** another context with the prescribed 96-bit signature.

**The exact payoff, corrected.** In swept-a0 units, cost per preimage = 2^32 + P^-1·X, with P = 2^-13.38 (R=20) and 2^-45.38 (R=21):
- R=20: floor **2^32 = 13.4 bits**, reached once X <~ 2^18.6. Break-even X = 2^32 (~5 A100-seconds). (The reported 2^14.4 is per-preimage only when all ~2^18.6 preimages of the same digest are harvested from one full fibre — a real number, but not the number for inverting one prescribed digest.)
- R=21: cost = 2^45.38·X, so **gain = 32 - log2(X) bits**. X = 1 gives 2^45.4 (the full ~30-bit target); X = 10 gives 2^48.7; X = 10^4 gives 2^58.7, still a 19-bit result and a paper. Break-even is again X = 2^32.
- Known achievable X: the m=2 birthday, X = 2^47.5, i.e. **15.5 bits the wrong side of break-even**, giving 2^60.9 at R=20 (matching elimination_search's independently derived 2^60.4) and 2^92.9 at R=21. Larger m is monotonically worse (m-collision on 96 bits costs 2^(96(m-1)/m)).

So the entire remaining question in this direction is one number: **can a context in a prescribed 96-bit fibre be produced in under ~2^32 swept-a0-equivalents?** Everything else — table geometry, resolution, root policy, k-list, MITM — is closed by the counting bound and the 0.099-bit multi-root ceiling and should not be touched again.

**The test, and why it is not the SAT test you already ran.** Tseitin-encode rounds 8–19 of the schedule with a12..a19 fixed by the digest and e8 = e9 = -1 (the map of `vecsig.py`), assert equality to a target on 96 bits, and measure seconds per solution with kissat/CaDiCaL and with a CP model — at w=12 and w=16 first, to get the scaling exponent, then w=32. The `sat_hybrid` study handed CDCL the whole preimage: an over-constrained instance with essentially one solution. This one is **under-constrained** — 128 bits of freedom against 96 bits of target, with 2^32 solutions guaranteed to exist and densely spread — which is the regime CDCL and local search are actually good at, and the one cost model in this project a solver could plausibly win. Cost: a few CPU-hours on the 28 cores, no GPU, no table build beyond a reduced-width relation table.

**Kill criterion, fixed in advance.** Fit log2(seconds per solution) against w over w=12,16 and extrapolate to 32. If the extrapolated X exceeds 2^32 swept-a0-equivalents (~5 A100-seconds; ~7 minutes on one CPU core at ~10^7 swept a0/s), the line is closed and R=21 stays at 2^77 — write that number into the barrier paper and stop. If X lands below 2^32, the gain at R=21 is 32 - log2(X) bits and it is the first crack in eight searches.

**My prediction: it fails**, and I would not bet against that prediction. The partial-match landscape is perfectly flat — contexts matching the low k bits of a prescribed signature track 2^(4w-k) at every k from 0 to 24, so there is nothing for propagation or local search to climb; single-bit sensitivity of (KC0, KC1, KC2, kappa3) to every free context word is 10.9–16.1 bits of 32 in all 16 cells (three independent measurements agree); fibre sizes are Poisson (chi^2 = 52.7 on 57 df, exhaustive at w=6); 0 of 50 fibres are closed under an affine XOR rule; the eight most frequent within-fibre shifts retest at 0.89–1.38x chance over all 2^24 contexts; and 0 of 9,600 single-bit flips left KC0, KC1, KC2 fixed. Beating the birthday needs a *structural* inversion of a 12-round ARX map, and every statistic says there is none. The reason to spend the afternoon anyway is that this is the only remaining place where a measurement could surprise us, the surprise is worth 19–32 bits, and the cost of finding out is a few CPU-hours against the alternative of writing "we predict" where the paper could say "we measured".

**Second, much weaker, also cheap (a few CPU-hours):** the wildcard study's own follow-up — compute the exact Walsh spectrum of c3 **on the attack's own distribution** (a1,a2,a3 supplied by real lookups, not free variables) at w=12–16, pooled over contexts, against a shuffled-candidate null. It is the only non-random signal found anywhere in the four studies, and it was measured on the wrong distribution. Upside is bounded and probably ~0.03 bits; the value is that it closes the linear/lattice line completely rather than at 20-bit subcubes.

**Do not run:** the MILP/PB test on the blasted system (answered by the wildcard study's CP-SAT ladder), further table geometry (closed by k >= 4.58), any further lattice embedding without first passing the screening test below, and the two-sided RX trail search (the 10.3-bit ceiling makes it moot even if it succeeded).

**Keep as a reusable instrument:** the lattice screening test. For any proposed embedding of any SHA-256 subproblem, compute dim L0 = N+1-rank(A), det = sqrt(det(A~A~^T)), gh = sqrt(dim/2·pi·e)·det^(1/dim), ratio = sqrt(N+1)/gh. Controls fix the decision boundary at 1.0; every SHA-256 formulation lands at 2.25–2.38, and the analytic value sqrt(4·pi·e)/2.5 = 2.34 says why. That makes any future lattice proposal falsifiable in minutes, and it is a good half-page of the barrier paper.
result.plain_english: Your instinct to ask about a lattice was a good one, and the answer is more interesting than a flat no. Everyone's expectation — including mine going in — was that SHA-256 simply cannot be written down as a lattice problem. That turns out to be false: it can be, exactly, with no approximation, because a single arithmetic identity (a+b+c = x+2m) captures XOR and majority-vote at the same time, so every piece of SHA-256 becomes a straightforward system of linear equations in variables that are each either 0 or 1. The trouble is what a lattice does next. Lattice reduction keeps the equations and throws away the fact that the variables must be 0 or 1 — and in an ARX design like SHA-256, that "must be 0 or 1" is where every bit of the difficulty lives, because it is what makes carries carries. The measurement is brutally clear: the true answer is nowhere near the shortest vector, roughly 2^76 lattice points are shorter than it for even the friendliest single equation in the attack, and about 2^2891 are shorter for the full system. Not "LLL is too weak" — a perfect oracle would fail too. And there is a deeper way to say the same thing: lattices break codes like truncated random-number generators because those hand you far more information than you need, whereas in a preimage the equations *are* the goal, with exactly as many constraint bits as unknown bits. There is no free redundancy to spend, and buying some costs precisely the 2^32 you were trying to delete. The other three angles — multi-dimensional tables, symmetry, and integer programming — each died at their own named place: a table would need at least five 32-bit axes because the whole computation depends on only five constants, so anything smaller answers "yes, maybe" in every cell; symmetry is capped at 10.3 bits before any experiment, because the groups available (32 rotations, 2 complementations, 20 round shifts) are simply too small, and in any case rotating a real SHA-256 round is impossible rather than merely unlikely — zero of all four billion possible first message words work; and integer programming or Gröbner bases price out at 2^50 seconds and 2^2601 respectively. All four end at the same wall you already know: a word gets fed back five rounds later through a one-input scrambler, and you cannot neutralise a one-input function by choosing something else, only by already knowing the input. The one place still worth an afternoon is not a lattice at all. When you sweep a context, the expensive part — the 2^32 candidates — depends on the context only through 96 bits of it, so a *second* context that agrees in those 96 bits would inherit the whole list for free and get an independent free shot at the final check. If such a second context could be produced in under about five seconds of GPU time, it would start removing bits; at 21 rounds, where the effect compounds, it could be worth anywhere from 19 to 32 bits, which is the whole prize. The catch is that producing one appears to cost a 96-bit search, and the best known route is about 15 bits too expensive. Every statistic we have says no shortcut exists — full avalanche, no structure in the near-misses, textbook-random fibre sizes — but that has never actually been handed to a SAT solver in the right shape, and a few CPU-hours would convert a prediction into a measurement. I would spend that afternoon and no more. One correction to carry forward: the advertised payoff of this idea at 20 rounds was overstated — one unavoidable sweep sets a floor, so it is worth 13 bits there, not 31; the 21-round figure is the honest one.
